newsitem.title: NORWAY: Norske Skog sees weaker 1997 result.
newsitem.headline: Norske Skog sees weaker 1997 result.

text.p: Norwegian forestry company Norske Skogindustrier ASA said on Thursday it saw weaker results this year than in 1996.
"The year 1996 was a good year for Norske Skog," a statement accompanying the 1996 profits announcement said.
"Norske Skog is expected to achieve a weaker result in 1997 than in 1996," it said.
The group booked a pre-tax profit of 1.73 billion crowns ($261.8 million) in 1996, compared to 2.34 billion crowns for the record year 1995.
"The result trend reflects the fact that the favourable market conditions at the start of 1996 gradually weakened during the year," the statement said.

"Norske Skog's paper mills achieved a record profit in 1996, offsetting weak results in pulp and sawn timber. During the year, the markets for printing paper also weakened. Pulp prices fell dramatically and the supply of sawn timber exceeded demand in Europe," it said.

The board proposed to pay a dividend of seven crowns per share, up from six crowns in 1995. The group booked a pre-tax profit of 1.73 billion crowns in 1996, compared to 2.34 billion crowns for the record year 1995.

The board proposed to pay a dividend of seven crowns per share, up from six crowns in 1995. The result, which beat market expectations, included operating revenues of 13.27 billion crowns, up from 12.55 billion in 1995.
Operating expenses came to 10.13 billion, up from 9.22 billion. Operating profits fell to 1.92 billion from 2.50 billion while after-tax profits shrank to 1.32 billion crowns from 1.70 billion.
The Paper division's operating result rose to 9.49 billion crowns from 8.07 billion, Building Materials increased to 2.58 billion from 2.33 billion while Fibre fell to 1.22 billion from 2.17 billion.

Norske Skog, Norway's biggest forestry group, said 1997 would be a year of consolidation in some segments of the world's printing paper industry until there was once again better balance between supply and demand. In the longer term, the total market is expected to grow by 2-3 percent per year, it said.

Growth in capacity for printing paper in Western Europe this year will come almost entirely from the upgrading of existing mills, and will amount to around two percent for newsprint and SC-quality magazine paper and four percent for LWC magazine paper, it said.

"At the turn of the year there were indications that the markets for newsprint and SC magazine paper will become firmer during 1997. There is still an imbalance in the market for these grades -- something which led to a relatively steep price decline around the turn of the year," the statement said.

"At the start of 1997 demand for LWC magazine paper and fine paper was developing favourably, and price increases are expected. This will have a positive impact on market pulp as well," Norske Skog said.
